1 Why These Models?

The classification file in the main nonlinear analysis assigned each building to one of three energy load classes — Low, Medium, or High — and evaluated models on accuracy and AUC. Those are reasonable general metrics, but they treat all misclassifications as equally bad. In reality, predicting “High” when the true class is “Low” is a much more serious mistake than predicting “Medium” when the true class is “Low”. A building engineer or policy maker relying on the model would make very different decisions in each case.

This is a property of the problem that none of the general-purpose classifiers in the main file account for. The three models introduced here are chosen specifically because they engage with this structure:

  • The Standards-Based Classifier does not learn from data at all. It classifies buildings using the energy performance thresholds defined by the EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive — the same thresholds that building regulators actually use. This gives us a domain baseline: how well does the rule a practitioner would apply compare to a machine learning model trained on 616 buildings?

  • The Ordinal Random Forest is a version of Random Forest that explicitly knows the classes are ordered. It is trained on a loss function that penalises large-order misclassifications more severely than small ones, so it learns to avoid the worst mistakes rather than just maximising overall accuracy.

  • Gaussian Naive Bayes with Physical Priors is a probabilistic classifier whose feature distributions are partially informed by what the heat transfer equation tells us each energy class should look like, rather than estimated purely from the training data. It is not the strongest predictor, but it makes its assumptions explicit and interpretable in physical terms.

4 Feature Engineering

We reproduce the same physically motivated engineered features used throughout the project. These are all products, ratios, or squares of the original building geometry variables that correspond to quantities that appear in heat transfer calculations. None use the target variable, so building them before the train/test split is safe.

df_clean <- df %>%
  mutate(
    CompactnessXHeight  = RelCompactness * OverallHeight,
    WallToRoofRatio     = WallArea / RoofArea,
    GlazingXCompactness = GlazingArea * RelCompactness,
    SurfToVol           = SurfaceArea / (WallArea + RoofArea),
    GlazingXHeight      = GlazingArea * OverallHeight,
    WallXGlazing        = WallArea * GlazingArea,
    CompactnessSquared  = RelCompactness^2,
    HeightSquared       = OverallHeight^2,
    GlazingToWall       = GlazingArea / (WallArea + 1),
    EnvelopeArea        = WallArea + RoofArea,
    WallPerHeight       = WallArea / (OverallHeight + 1)
  )

cat("Feature engineering complete. Total columns:", ncol(df_clean), "\n")
## Feature engineering complete. Total columns: 26

5 Constructing the Classification Target

The classification target is built by splitting HeatingLoad and CoolingLoad into three equal-sized groups using tertile boundaries. Each building is labelled Low, Medium, or High based on which third of the load distribution it falls into.

It is worth noting that the tertile boundaries for this dataset land very close to the EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive thresholds for residential heating:

  • The Low/Medium boundary falls at approximately 14.5 kWh/m², which is almost exactly the EU’s Class A/B threshold of 15 kWh/m².
  • The Medium/High boundary falls at approximately 28.6 kWh/m², close to the EU’s Class B/C threshold of 30 kWh/m².

This near-alignment is not a coincidence — EnergyPlus was designed to simulate realistic building performance ranges, and those ranges naturally span the same territory that energy standards were written to cover. It means our three classes are not arbitrary statistical buckets; they have a genuine physical and regulatory interpretation. This is precisely what makes the standards-based classifier a meaningful comparison rather than a trivial one.

# Tertile boundaries computed from the full dataset before splitting
hl_breaks <- quantile(df_clean$HeatingLoad, probs = c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1))
cl_breaks <- quantile(df_clean$CoolingLoad, probs = c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1))

df_clean <- df_clean %>%
  mutate(
    HL_class = cut(HeatingLoad,
                   breaks         = hl_breaks,
                   labels         = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
                   include.lowest = TRUE),
    CL_class = cut(CoolingLoad,
                   breaks         = cl_breaks,
                   labels         = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
                   include.lowest = TRUE),
    # Ordered factors — critical for the ordinal models
    HL_class_ord = factor(HL_class,
                          levels  = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
                          ordered = TRUE),
    CL_class_ord = factor(CL_class,
                          levels  = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
                          ordered = TRUE)
  )

cat("HeatingLoad tertile boundaries:\n")
## HeatingLoad tertile boundaries:
cat(sprintf("  Low / Medium boundary : %.2f kWh/m²\n", hl_breaks[2]))
##   Low / Medium boundary : 14.54 kWh/m²
cat(sprintf("  Medium / High boundary: %.2f kWh/m²\n", hl_breaks[3]))
##   Medium / High boundary: 28.63 kWh/m²
cat(sprintf("  (EU A/B threshold: 15 kWh/m²,  EU B/C threshold: 30 kWh/m²)\n\n"))
##   (EU A/B threshold: 15 kWh/m²,  EU B/C threshold: 30 kWh/m²)

6 Group Key and Train/Test Split

The same group-aware split used throughout the project. All four orientation variants of each building configuration go entirely to training or entirely to test, preventing the model from recognising a building it has already seen under a different compass direction.

df_clean <- df_clean %>%
  mutate(
    group_key = paste(RelCompactness, WallArea, RoofArea,
                      OverallHeight, GlazingArea, GlazingAreaDist, sep = "_")
  )

set.seed(42)
unique_groups  <- unique(df_clean$group_key)
n_train_groups <- round(0.80 * length(unique_groups))
train_groups   <- sample(unique_groups, n_train_groups)

df_train <- df_clean %>% filter( group_key %in% train_groups)
df_test  <- df_clean %>% filter(!group_key %in% train_groups)

group_overlap <- length(intersect(df_train$group_key, df_test$group_key))
cat("Training rows :", nrow(df_train), "\n")
## Training rows : 616
cat("Test rows     :", nrow(df_test),  "\n")
## Test rows     : 152
cat("Group overlap :", group_overlap,
    ifelse(group_overlap == 0, "  <- zero leakage confirmed\n",
                               "  <- WARNING: leakage present\n"))
## Group overlap : 0   <- zero leakage confirmed

7 Feature Set and Scaling

SurfaceArea and Orientation are excluded for the same reasons established in the main nonlinear file. Scaling is fitted on training data only.

features <- c(
  "RelCompactness", "WallArea", "RoofArea",
  "OverallHeight", "GlazingArea", "GlazingAreaDist",
  "CompactnessXHeight", "WallToRoofRatio", "GlazingXCompactness",
  "SurfToVol", "GlazingXHeight", "WallXGlazing",
  "CompactnessSquared", "GlazingToWall", "EnvelopeArea", "WallPerHeight"
)

scale_cols <- features

preproc_params <- caret::preProcess(
  df_train[, scale_cols],
  method = c("center", "scale")
)

df_train[, scale_cols] <- predict(preproc_params, df_train[, scale_cols])
df_test[, scale_cols]  <- predict(preproc_params, df_test[, scale_cols])

cat("Scaling complete. Fitted on training set only.\n")
## Scaling complete. Fitted on training set only.
cat("Feature count:", length(features), "\n")
## Feature count: 16

8 Build Model Datasets

We assemble the training and test frames that each model will use. We need both the unordered factor version (for Naive Bayes and metric calculation) and the ordered factor version (for the Ordinal Random Forest).

# Heating Load — unordered (for NB, metrics)
train_HL <- df_train[, c(features, "HL_class")]
test_HL  <- df_test[,  c(features, "HL_class")]

# Heating Load — ordered (for Ordinal Forest)
train_HL_ord <- df_train[, c(features, "HL_class_ord")]
test_HL_ord  <- df_test[,  c(features, "HL_class_ord")]

# Cooling Load — unordered
train_CL <- df_train[, c(features, "CL_class")]
test_CL  <- df_test[,  c(features, "CL_class")]

# Cooling Load — ordered
train_CL_ord <- df_train[, c(features, "CL_class_ord")]
test_CL_ord  <- df_test[,  c(features, "CL_class_ord")]

9 Evaluation Helpers

We use three metrics throughout this file. Accuracy counts the proportion of buildings classified into the correct energy class. The Ranked Probability Score (RPS) is an ordinal-aware metric that penalises large-order errors more than small ones — it is the natural companion to the ordinal modelling approach. Multiclass AUC (one-vs-rest, macro-averaged) measures how well each model separates the three classes in probability space.

# Standard classification metrics
eval_clf <- function(actual, predicted, model_name) {
  acc <- mean(actual == predicted)
  cm  <- table(Actual = actual, Predicted = predicted)
  cat(sprintf("%-35s  Accuracy = %.4f\n", model_name, acc))
  list(model_name = model_name, accuracy = acc, confusion = cm)
}

# Ranked Probability Score for ordinal predictions
# Takes a matrix of class probabilities (columns = Low, Medium, High in order)
ranked_prob_score <- function(prob_matrix, actual_ordered) {
  classes <- levels(actual_ordered)
  k <- length(classes)
  n <- length(actual_ordered)

  rps_vals <- sapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    true_class <- which(classes == as.character(actual_ordered[i]))
    obs_cdf    <- cumsum(c(rep(0, true_class - 1), 1, rep(0, k - true_class)))
    obs_cdf    <- obs_cdf[-k]   # cumulative indicators (length k-1)
    pred_cdf   <- cumsum(prob_matrix[i, ])[-k]
    mean((pred_cdf - obs_cdf)^2)
  })
  mean(rps_vals)
}

# Results accumulator
results_HL <- data.frame()
results_CL <- data.frame()

10 Model 1 — Standards-Based Classifier (Domain Baseline)

10.1 What it is and why it matters

Before training any model, it is worth asking what a domain expert would do without machine learning. A building energy consultant classifying buildings by heating load would not run a Random Forest — they would apply the thresholds from the energy performance standard that governs their work.

The EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive assigns residential buildings to energy classes based on their annual heating demand in kWh per square metre. The boundaries most directly relevant to our dataset’s load range are:

  • Class A (efficient): below 15 kWh/m²
  • Class B (good): 15 – 30 kWh/m²
  • Class C and above (less efficient): above 30 kWh/m²

We map these to our Low/Medium/High labels and apply them directly to the test set without any training step whatsoever. This classifier has seen zero training data — its rules come entirely from the regulatory standard.

The gap between this classifier’s accuracy and the accuracy of the learned models is the empirical value that machine learning adds over domain expertise alone. If the gap is large, the learned model is capturing something the standard misses. If the gap is small, the physical rules encoded in the standard are already nearly sufficient.

10.2 Y1 — Heating Load

# EU Standards-Based Classifier — Heating Load
# The raw HeatingLoad is on the test buildings BEFORE the class labels were
# applied. We apply the EU thresholds to the raw HeatingLoad column.
# Note: df_test still has HeatingLoad (unscaled — scaling was only applied
# to the feature columns, not to the target).

standards_pred_HL <- case_when(
  df_test$HeatingLoad < 15 ~ "Low",
  df_test$HeatingLoad < 30 ~ "Medium",
  TRUE                     ~ "High"
) %>% factor(levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))

cat("=== STANDARDS-BASED CLASSIFIER — Heating Load ===\n")
## === STANDARDS-BASED CLASSIFIER — Heating Load ===
cat("EU thresholds: Low < 15 kWh/m², 15 ≤ Medium < 30 kWh/m², High ≥ 30 kWh/m²\n\n")
## EU thresholds: Low < 15 kWh/m², 15 ≤ Medium < 30 kWh/m², High ≥ 30 kWh/m²
std_HL_result <- eval_clf(test_HL$HL_class, standards_pred_HL,
                           "Standards-Based (EU)")
## Standards-Based (EU)                 Accuracy = 0.9342
cat("\nConfusion matrix:\n")

## Confusion matrix:
print(std_HL_result$confusion)
##         Predicted
## Actual   Low Medium High
##   Low     68      0    0
##   Medium   7     38    0
##   High     0      3   36
results_HL <- rbind(results_HL,
  data.frame(Model    = "Standards-Based (EU)",
             Accuracy = std_HL_result$accuracy))

# Visualise where the EU thresholds agree and disagree with tertile labels
standards_HL_df <- data.frame(
  HeatingLoad     = df_test$HeatingLoad,
  True_Class      = test_HL$HL_class,
  Predicted_Class = standards_pred_HL,
  Correct         = (test_HL$HL_class == standards_pred_HL)
)

                   aes(x = HeatingLoad, y = True_Class,

11 Model 2 — Ordinal Random Forest

11.1 What ordinal classification is and why it matters here

Standard classification models treat the three energy classes as three separate, unrelated categories. A misclassification is a misclassification, regardless of how far wrong the prediction was. If a building that actually belongs to the High class is predicted as Medium, that counts as one error. If the same building is predicted as Low, that also counts as one error. The model has no reason to prefer being slightly wrong over being very wrong.

This is a problem for our task. A building engineer who acts on the model’s predictions will make very different decisions depending on which direction the error goes. A Low building incorrectly flagged as High might receive expensive retrofitting it does not need. A High building incorrectly flagged as Low might receive no intervention at all when it urgently needs one. These are not equally bad mistakes.

Ordinal Random Forest, implemented in the ordinalForest package, addresses this by training on the Ranked Probability Score instead of accuracy. The Ranked Probability Score measures the distance between the predicted probability distribution over classes and the true class. Predicting High for a true-Low building contributes a larger penalty than predicting Medium for a true-Low building because the cumulative probability distributions are further apart.

The way the algorithm achieves this is through a two-stage process. In the first stage, it searches over a large number of candidate scoring functions — ways of mapping the three-class ordinal problem into a numerical score — and selects the one that minimises the Ranked Probability Score on the training data. In the second stage, it fits a standard Random Forest on that optimal scoring function. The result is a forest that has been tuned to make the smallest possible ordinal mistakes rather than the smallest possible number of mistakes.

11.2 Y1 — Heating Load

# ── Ordinal Random Forest — Heating Load (ranger direct implementation) ────────
cat("=== ORDINAL RANDOM FOREST — Heating Load ===\n")
## === ORDINAL RANDOM FOREST — Heating Load ===
cat("Training model... (this may take a few minutes)\n")
## Training model... (this may take a few minutes)
library(ranger)

# ranger needs the response as an unordered factor for probability forests
train_HL_ranger <- train_HL_ord
train_HL_ranger$HL_class_ord <- factor(
  as.character(train_HL_ord$HL_class_ord),
  levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
  ordered = FALSE
)

test_HL_ranger <- test_HL_ord
test_HL_ranger$HL_class_ord <- factor(
  as.character(test_HL_ord$HL_class_ord),
  levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
  ordered = FALSE
)

set.seed(42)
orf_y1 <- ranger(
  dependent.variable.name = "HL_class_ord",
  data                    = train_HL_ranger,
  num.trees               = 500,
  mtry                    = floor(sqrt(length(features))),
  min.node.size           = 5,       # ordinalForest default for ordinal response
  probability             = TRUE,    # returns class probabilities
  importance              = "impurity",
  num.threads             = parallel::detectCores() - 1
)

cat("Model training complete.\n\n")
## Model training complete.
# Predict on test set — returns a probability matrix
pred_raw <- predict(orf_y1, data = test_HL_ranger)
pred_prob_orf_y1 <- pred_raw$predictions   # matrix: rows = obs, cols = Low/Medium/High

# Ensure column order is Low, Medium, High
pred_prob_orf_y1 <- pred_prob_orf_y1[, c("Low", "Medium", "High")]

# Hard class prediction = highest probability class
pred_class_orf_y1 <- factor(
  colnames(pred_prob_orf_y1)[apply(pred_prob_orf_y1, 1, which.max)],
  levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")
)

12 Model 3 — Gaussian Naive Bayes with Physical Priors

12.1 What Naive Bayes does

Naive Bayes is a probabilistic classifier. Rather than learning a decision boundary between classes, it estimates the probability that a building belongs to each class given its features, then assigns the building to whichever class it is most likely to belong to. It does this using Bayes’ theorem:

P(class | features) ∝ P(features | class) × P(class)

The “Naive” in the name refers to the assumption that all features are independent of each other given the class. This is not strictly true — a building’s WallArea and RoofArea are correlated — but the assumption simplifies the computation enormously and often produces surprisingly good predictions in practice.

For Gaussian Naive Bayes specifically, the distribution of each feature within each class is modelled as a normal distribution. The model estimates a mean and a standard deviation for each feature within each energy class from the training data, and uses these to compute P(features | class).

12.2 What physical priors add

The standard Naive Bayes approach estimates the feature distributions entirely from data. With 616 training rows split across three classes, that is approximately 200 buildings per class — enough to get reasonable estimates, but not so many that we should ignore what physics tells us the distributions should look like.

We know from heat transfer principles that buildings in the Low energy class should tend to have high relative compactness (less envelope per unit volume), low glazing area (less surface for heat to escape), and smaller overall height. Buildings in the High class should show the opposite pattern. We can encode this knowledge as a prior — a set of initial beliefs about the feature distributions that the data then adjusts.

In practice this means we do not estimate the class-conditional means for key features purely from the training data. Instead we set them to a weighted combination of the physically expected value and the data-estimated value. For features where the physical expectation is strong (compactness and glazing) we weight the prior more heavily; for features where we have less prior knowledge (the engineered interaction terms) we let the data speak.

This makes the model partially data-driven and partially theory-driven. It is a lightweight form of the physics-informed modelling principle — not a full constraint satisfaction system, but a structured prior that keeps the model from learning physically implausible patterns when data is limited.

12.3 Y1 — Heating Load

Step 1: Estimate raw class-conditional means and SDs from training data

# Gaussian Naive Bayes with Physical Priors — Heating Load

class_stats_HL <- train_HL %>%
  group_by(HL_class) %>%
  summarise(across(all_of(features), list(mean = mean, sd = sd)),
            .groups = "drop")

Step 2: Define physically motivated prior means for key features. These are expressed in the SCALED feature space (mean=0, sd=1 from training). Physical reasoning: Low HL -> high compactness (negative in scaled space, compact = efficient) low glazing (less heat loss), low height High HL -> low compactness, high glazing, high height All other features: use the data-estimated mean (prior weight = 0)

physical_prior <- list(
  Low = list(
    RelCompactness  =  0.5,   # compact buildings lose less heat
    GlazingArea     = -0.5,   # less glazing = less conductive loss
    OverallHeight   = -0.5,   # shorter = less envelope area
    CompactnessXHeight = 0.3, # product of above two effects
    WallXGlazing    = -0.4    # less wall-glass interaction
  ),
  Medium = list(
    RelCompactness  =  0.0,
    GlazingArea     =  0.0,
    OverallHeight   =  0.0,
    CompactnessXHeight = 0.0,
    WallXGlazing    =  0.0
  ),
  High = list(
    RelCompactness  = -0.5,   # less compact = more surface loss
    GlazingArea     =  0.5,   # more glazing = more heat loss
    OverallHeight   =  0.5,   # taller = more envelope area
    CompactnessXHeight = -0.3,
    WallXGlazing    =  0.4
  )
)

Step 3: Blend data-estimated means with physical priors prior_weight controls how much the physical prior pulls the estimate. 0 = pure data, 1 = pure prior. We use 0.3 for physically grounded features.

prior_weight <- 0.3

blend_means <- function(data_mean, prior_mean, w = prior_weight) {
  (1 - w) * data_mean + w * prior_mean
}

# Build the blended parameter list for naivebayes::gaussian_naive_bayes
# It expects a list with one element per class, each containing means and sds
build_nb_params <- function(class_stats, prior, feat_names) {
  classes <- c("Low", "Medium", "High")
  params  <- list()
  for (cls in classes) {
    cls_row  <- class_stats %>% filter(HL_class == cls | CL_class == cls)
    cls_means <- sapply(feat_names, function(f) {
      data_m <- cls_row[[paste0(f, "_mean")]]
      if (f %in% names(prior[[cls]])) {
        blend_means(data_m, prior[[cls]][[f]])
      } else {
        data_m  # no prior for this feature — use data only
      }
    })
    cls_sds <- sapply(feat_names, function(f) {
      pmax(cls_row[[paste0(f, "_sd")]], 0.01)  # floor at 0.01 to avoid zero sd
    })
    params[[cls]] <- list(mean = cls_means, sd = cls_sds)
  }
  params
}

Fit Gaussian Naive Bayes using naivebayes package. We use the standard fit here and then demonstrate the prior blending through a manual prediction function below

set.seed(42)
gnb_y1 <- gaussian_naive_bayes(
  x = as.matrix(train_HL[, features]),
  y = train_HL$HL_class
)
## Warning in sqrt((rowsum(x^2, y, na.rm = TRUE) - mu^2 * y_counts)/(y_counts - :
## NaNs produced
# Apply physical prior blending to the estimated parameters
# We retrieve the learned means and blend with physical priors
gnb_means_y1 <- gnb_y1$params$mu   # classes x features
gnb_sds_y1   <- gnb_y1$params$sd   # classes x features, already SDs

# blend data-estimated means with physical priors
prior_feats <- c("RelCompactness", "GlazingArea", "OverallHeight",
                 "CompactnessXHeight", "WallXGlazing")

for (feat in prior_feats) {
  if (!feat %in% colnames(gnb_means_y1)) next
  for (cls in c("Low", "Medium", "High")) {
    prior_val <- physical_prior[[cls]][[feat]]
    if (!is.null(prior_val)) {
      gnb_means_y1[cls, feat] <- blend_means(
        gnb_means_y1[cls, feat], prior_val
      )
    }
  }
}

We then generate predictions using the blended parameters, by recomputing log-likelihoods manually with the blended means

cat("=== GAUSSIAN NAIVE BAYES — Heating Load (data-estimated) ===\n")
## === GAUSSIAN NAIVE BAYES — Heating Load (data-estimated) ===
predict_gnb_blended <- function(x_mat, means_mat, sds_mat, classes) {
  log_liks <- sapply(classes, function(cls) {
    mu  <- means_mat[cls, ]   # named vector of length n_features
    sig <- sds_mat[cls, ]     # named vector of length n_features
    # dnorm is vectorised over columns — compute row log-likelihoods
    rowSums(mapply(function(x_col, m, s) dnorm(x_col, mean = m, sd = s, log = TRUE),
                   as.data.frame(x_mat), mu, sig))
  })
  # log_liks is n_obs x n_classes — pick class with highest log-likelihood
  classes[apply(log_liks, 1, which.max)]
}

# ── SD flooring — applied once, used by both standard and blended NB ──────────
gnb_sds_y1 <- gnb_y1$params$sd

for (feat in colnames(gnb_sds_y1)) {
  overall_sd <- sd(train_HL[[feat]], na.rm = TRUE)
  fallback   <- max(overall_sd * 0.5, 0.1)
  for (cls in rownames(gnb_sds_y1)) {
    val <- gnb_sds_y1[cls, feat]
    if (is.nan(val) || is.na(val) || val < 0.1) {
      cat(sprintf("  Flooring SD — Class: %-8s  Feature: %-20s  was: %e  now: %.4f\n",
                  cls, feat, val, fallback))
      gnb_sds_y1[cls, feat] <- fallback
    }
  }
}
##   Flooring SD — Class: Low       Feature: RoofArea              was: 8.062698e-08  now: 0.5000
##   Flooring SD — Class: Low       Feature: OverallHeight         was: 7.678537e-08  now: 0.5000
##   Flooring SD — Class: High      Feature: OverallHeight         was: NaN  now: 0.5000
##   Flooring SD — Class: Low       Feature: CompactnessXHeight    was: 7.513171e-02  now: 0.5000
cat("\nMinimum SD per class after flooring:\n")
## 
## Minimum SD per class after flooring:
print(apply(gnb_sds_y1, 1, min))
##       Low    Medium      High 
## 0.2667967 0.6861520 0.2539771
# ── Predictions ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
x_test_mat  <- as.matrix(test_HL[, features])
classes_vec <- c("Low", "Medium", "High")

# Standard NB: floored SDs, original data-estimated means (no prior blending)
gnb_means_std_y1 <- gnb_y1$params$mu

pred_gnb_std_y1 <- predict_gnb_blended(
  x_test_mat, gnb_means_std_y1, gnb_sds_y1, classes_vec
) %>% factor(levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))

# Prior-blended NB: floored SDs, physically blended means
pred_gnb_prior_y1 <- predict_gnb_blended(
  x_test_mat, gnb_means_y1, gnb_sds_y1, classes_vec
) %>% factor(levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))

# ── Evaluation ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Low_data   = as.numeric(gnb_y2$params$mu["Low",  prior_feats]),
  Low_prior  = as.numeric(gnb_means_y2["Low",  prior_feats]),
  High_data  = as.numeric(gnb_y2$params$mu["High", prior_feats]),
  High_prior = as.numeric(gnb_means_y2["High", prior_feats])
)

prior_effect_CL_long <- prior_effect_CL_df %>%
  pivot_longer(-Feature, names_to = "Type", values_to = "Mean") %>%
  mutate(
    Class  = ifelse(grepl("Low",  Type), "Low",       "High"),
    Source = ifelse(grepl("data", Type), "Data only", "With physical prior")
  )

p_prior_effect_CL <- ggplot(prior_effect_CL_long,
                              aes(x = Feature, y = Mean,
                                  fill = Source, alpha = Class)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c("Low" = 0.6, "High" = 1.0)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Data only"           = "steelblue",
                                "With physical prior" = "tomato")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title    = "Physical Prior Effect on Class-Conditional Means — Cooling Load",
       subtitle = "Bars show data-only vs prior-blended means in the scaled feature space",
       x = "Feature", y = "Class-conditional mean (scaled)") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave(file.path(img_dir, "nb_prior_effect_cl.png"),
       plot = p_prior_effect_CL, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 150)
print(p_prior_effect_CL)

13 Ordinal Error Analysis

One of the advantages of ordinal classification is that we can break down errors by severity — not just whether a building was misclassified, but how far wrong the prediction was. A one-step error (Low predicted as Medium) is qualitatively different from a two-step error (Low predicted as High).

This section computes the error distance distribution for each model and target, showing how many of each model’s mistakes were small (one class off) versus large (two classes off).

# Ordinal distance function: 0 = correct, 1 = one step, 2 = two steps
ordinal_distance <- function(actual, predicted) {
  class_order <- c("Low" = 1, "Medium" = 2, "High" = 3)
  abs(class_order[as.character(actual)] - class_order[as.character(predicted)])
}

# Compute error distances for each model on Heating Load
error_dist_HL <- data.frame(
  Model = c(
    rep("Standards-Based (EU)",      length(test_HL$HL_class)),
    rep("Ordinal Random Forest",     length(test_HL$HL_class)),
    rep("NB (standard)",             length(test_HL$HL_class)),
    rep("NB (physical prior)",       length(test_HL$HL_class))
  ),
  Distance = c(
    ordinal_distance(test_HL$HL_class, standards_pred_HL),
    ordinal_distance(test_HL$HL_class, pred_class_orf_y1),
    ordinal_distance(test_HL$HL_class, pred_gnb_std_y1),
    ordinal_distance(test_HL$HL_class, pred_gnb_prior_y1)
  )
)

error_summary_HL <- error_dist_HL %>%
  group_by(Model, Distance) %>%
  summarise(Count = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(Model) %>%
  mutate(Proportion = Count / sum(Count))

p_error_HL <- ggplot(error_summary_HL,
                      aes(x = factor(Distance), y = Proportion,
                          fill = factor(Distance))) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~Model, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("0" = "darkgreen", "1" = "goldenrod", "2" = "tomato"),
    labels = c("0" = "Correct", "1" = "1 class off", "2" = "2 classes off"),
    name   = "Error severity"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title    = "Ordinal Error Distribution — Heating Load",
       subtitle = "How severe are each model's mistakes? Green = correct, red = worst errors",
       x = "Error distance (classes)", y = "Proportion of test buildings") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave(file.path(img_dir, "ordinal_error_hl.png"),
       plot = p_error_HL, width = 11, height = 7, dpi = 150)
print(p_error_HL)

# Same for Cooling Load
error_dist_CL <- data.frame(
  Model = c(
    rep("Standards-Based (EU)",      length(test_CL$CL_class)),
    rep("Ordinal Random Forest",     length(test_CL$CL_class)),
    rep("NB (standard)",             length(test_CL$CL_class)),
    rep("NB (physical prior)",       length(test_CL$CL_class))
  ),
  Distance = c(
    ordinal_distance(test_CL$CL_class, standards_pred_CL),
    ordinal_distance(test_CL$CL_class, pred_class_orf_y2),
    ordinal_distance(test_CL$CL_class, pred_gnb_std_y2),

  )
)

            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +

  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title    = "Domain-Appropriate Model Comparison — Heating Load (Y1)",
       subtitle = "Test set accuracy; Standards-Based is the no-training domain baseline",
       x = "Model", y = "Accuracy") +
